assumptions: That the alert corresponded to a genuine increase in errors is assumed, not verified — no metric or log evidence was obtained to support it.
That the incident ended when the alert closed is assumed from the alert lifecycle alone, not from observed recovery of the service.
The absence of returned metrics is assumed to be a data-retrieval problem rather than a true absence of traffic; neither was confirmed.
No log lines were read and no remediation actions were attempted, so the service's actual state during the window is unknown.
input.executive_summary: An automated alert reported an elevated rate of failed requests on one of our internal services. The on-call automation picked it up and began investigating within a second, but when it asked for the service's recent performance data, none came back. With nothing to confirm or rule out customer-visible errors, the automation stopped rather than guess and handed the incident to human responders. The alert cleared on its own almost immediately after opening. No customer impact has been confirmed, and none has been ruled out either — we cannot say who, if anyone, was affected, because the data for the period in question could not be read. No configuration was changed, no service was restarted, and no fix was applied.
input.root_cause: Not determined. The alert fired and an investigation began immediately, but the metrics query for the incident window returned no data, so there was no evidence to distinguish a real error spike from a bad or premature alert; the investigator produced no candidate cause and the incident was escalated to humans. The only concrete finding is the absence of metrics for the window — whether that is a retention/indexing lag, an anchor-time window that closed before data was written, or a metrics-pipeline failure was not established.
